subsection: 2. US foreign policy, 1945–1972: Berlin, Korea, Cuba and Vietnam

notes.h: Internationalism, imperialism and the Cold War background
notes.b: Before 1941 the United States kept out of most quarrels in Europe and Asia. The Second World War ended that, and by 1945 it faced a rival superpower, the Soviet Union, whose system was the opposite of its own.
points: Pre-war US isolationism (staying out of other countries' conflicts) was ended by Pearl Harbor and the war, so after 1945 the United States followed internationalism: active involvement in world affairs instead of withdrawal.
The war left the United States the richest industrial power and, until the Soviet test in 1949, the only atomic power, which gave it the means to lead a worldwide policy.

The wartime alliance with the Soviet Union broke down because Soviet forces held Eastern Europe at the war's end; the strain showed at the Yalta conference (February 1945) and the Potsdam conference (July to August 1945).
Churchill's "iron curtain" speech at Fulton, Missouri, in March 1946 gave the division of Europe between East and West its best-known image.
The Cold War rested on a clash of systems: communism, with the state controlling the economy under one party, against capitalism, with private ownership and markets.
In China a civil war was being fought between Mao Zedong's Communists and Chiang Kai-shek's Nationalists, so Asia was drawn into the same contest as Europe.
Imperialism means domination of one country by another through political, military or economic control. In this topic it is applied to US influence in Cuba and to Soviet control of Eastern Europe.

Germany, and Berlin within it, was divided into four occupation zones or sectors (US, British, French and Soviet). Berlin lay deep inside the Soviet zone, so the three Western sectors, which became West Berlin, were cut off from the West by Soviet-held territory.

notes.h: Containment: the atomic bomb and Kennan's ideas
notes.b: Containment means checking Soviet and communist expansion by firm resistance. It grew out of a new weapon and one diplomat's analysis of how the Soviet Union behaved.
points: The atomic bombs were dropped on Hiroshima on 6 August 1945 and Nagasaki on 9 August 1945, on Truman's authority, which left the United States as the only country with atomic weapons.
The Soviet Union tested its own bomb on 29 August 1949, which ended the American monopoly, so the United States could no longer rely on the bomb alone to hold Soviet power back.
George Kennan, a US diplomat in Moscow, sent his Long Telegram in February 1946, arguing that Soviet expansion could be checked by firm, long-term resistance rather than by negotiation.
Kennan's article "The Sources of Soviet Conduct", published in Foreign Affairs in July 1947 under the signature X, made the same case in public and gave containment its name.

Keep four terms apart: containment is the idea (Kennan), the Truman Doctrine is political and military aid to Greece and Turkey, the Marshall Plan is economic aid to Western Europe, and NATO is the alliance.
notes.tip: Examiners expect each of these four to be tied to its own purpose. Don't call the Marshall Plan containment's first step or the Truman Doctrine an alliance.

notes.h: From the Truman Doctrine to NSC-68
notes.b: Between 1947 and 1950 a run of crises turned Kennan's idea into American policy and open commitments.
points: In February 1947 Britain told the United States it could no longer support Greece and Turkey, so Washington decided to take over that burden.

In the Truman Doctrine speech to Congress on 12 March 1947 Truman asked for about 400 million dollars for Greece and Turkey and committed the United States to support free peoples resisting armed minorities or outside pressure.
The Communist seizure of power in Czechoslovakia in February 1948 convinced many in Washington and Western Europe that the Soviet threat was immediate, so it made them readier to act.

Mao Zedong proclaimed the People's Republic of China on 1 October 1949. Republicans asked "Who lost China?" and used the question to attack Truman's Asia policy, which made it harder for him to look weak abroad.

NSC-68, a paper by the National Security Council (the President's foreign-policy advisory body), called in April 1950 for a large rise in defence spending to meet the Soviet threat. It was approved as policy in autumn 1950, after the Korean War began.
notes.tip: Date NSC-68 carefully: the paper is April 1950, but it became policy only after the Korean War began.

notes.b: Containment in Western Europe had an economic side. American money would rebuild damaged economies so that poverty and unrest did not push voters towards communism.
points: George Marshall, the Secretary of State, proposed a European recovery programme in a speech at Harvard University on 5 June 1947.
The European Recovery Program, passed by Congress in April 1948, provided about 13 billion dollars of aid to Western European countries between 1948 and 1952.
The plan had three aims: economic recovery in Western Europe, stopping the spread of communism, and rebuilding European markets for American goods.
Most aid was given as grants of food, fuel and machinery rather than as loans, so recipients received supplies they did not have to repay as ordinary debt.
The Organisation for European Economic Co-operation (OEEC) was set up in April 1948 to allocate the aid, and Britain, France and West Germany were the largest recipients.

The Soviet Union refused Marshall aid and pressed its satellite states (the Eastern European countries it controlled) to refuse too. Czechoslovakia first accepted, then withdrew in July 1947 under Soviet pressure, so Europe settled more firmly into two blocs.
notes.tip: Treat Marshall aid as foreign policy here, with its three aims and the Soviet refusal. There is more on Marshall aid as economic financing in the notes on the US economy 1945 to 1968.

notes.b: Aid was matched by a military guarantee. In 1949 the defence of Western Europe and the future of Germany were both settled in ways that made the division of Europe harder to undo.
points: The North Atlantic Treaty was signed on 4 April 1949 by twelve countries, including the United States, Britain, France, Canada and Italy.

NATO, founded in April 1949 on the Article 5 principle of collective defence, was the first peacetime alliance of its kind that the United States had joined, a clear break from pre-war isolationism and a sign that internationalism now meant permanent commitments.
Article 5 of the treaty stated that an armed attack on one member would be treated as an attack on all, which is the basis of collective defence: any attacker would face the whole alliance.

Germany was divided as well: the Federal Republic of Germany (West Germany) was founded in May 1949 in the Western zones, and the German Democratic Republic (East Germany) followed in October 1949 in the Soviet zone.

notes.h: Berlin, 1948 to 1949: the blockade and the airlift
notes.b: Berlin lay inside the Soviet zone, so the Soviet Union could squeeze the Western sectors without invading. The crisis of 1948 to 1949 tested whether the West would stay.
points: The Soviet Union began blocking road, rail and canal access to West Berlin on 24 June 1948, aiming to force the Western powers out of the city.
The Western powers responded with an airlift that flew food, coal and other supplies into West Berlin. More than two million tons were carried before the blockade was lifted on 12 May 1949.
Truman chose the airlift rather than an armed convoy because forcing a way through by road would have risked fighting Soviet troops and starting a war.
The result was a Western success: the Soviet Union lifted the blockade without achieving its aim, and the West held Berlin without firing a shot.
notes.tip: The airlift as a success without firing a shot is the usual point examiners reward. Give the cause (the blockade), the Western response and its result.

notes.h: Berlin, 1958 to 1963: the ultimatum, the Wall and Kennedy's visit
notes.b: Berlin remained a flashpoint after the airlift. From 1958 the Soviet leader pressed the West to leave, and in 1961 the border between East and West Berlin was sealed.
points: In November 1958 Khrushchev demanded that the Western powers withdraw from Berlin within six months, and the issue was debated at the Vienna summit with Kennedy in June 1961.
More than two million East Germans had fled to the West between 1949 and 1961, mostly by crossing from East to West Berlin, which drained the East's skilled workforce.
The Berlin Wall was built from 13 August 1961, closing the border between East and West Berlin and stopping the flow of refugees.
In October 1961 American and Soviet tanks faced each other at Checkpoint Charlie, the crossing point for foreigners, in a tense standoff that ended without shots.
The Wall was a propaganda defeat for the East, because it had to wall in its own people, but the West accepted it rather than tearing it down, so the division of the city became permanent.
Kennedy visited West Berlin on 26 June 1963 and declared in German "Ich bin ein Berliner" (I am a Berliner), a statement of solidarity that was widely praised in the West.
notes.tip: Keep the three Berlin episodes apart: the blockade (1948 to 1949), Khrushchev's ultimatum (1958) and the Wall (1961). Say more than two million refugees, never an exact total.

notes.h: Korea: causes and the outbreak of war, 1945 to 1950
notes.b: Korea was split by the superpowers in 1945. In 1950 the split turned into war, and the United States fought under the flag of the United Nations.
points: Korea was divided at the 38th parallel in 1945. The Republic of Korea in the South under Syngman Rhee and the Democratic People's Republic in the North under Kim Il Sung were both founded in 1948.

US troops left South Korea in 1949, and Secretary of State Dean Acheson's speech of January 1950 placed Korea outside the American defence perimeter in the Pacific. It may have encouraged the North, though historians disagree how far.
North Korean forces invaded the South on 25 June 1950. The UN Security Council condemned the attack and recommended that members help South Korea repel it.
The Council could act because the Soviet delegate was absent (the Soviet Union was boycotting it), so there was no Soviet veto, and this is why the war was fought as a UN operation.
Truman sent American forces without asking Congress for a declaration of war and described the operation as a police action, so the war was never formally declared.

Korea applied containment to Asia: Washington saw the invasion as communist expansion that had to be stopped, as the domino theory (if one country falls to communism, its neighbours follow) later argued in Vietnam.
notes.tip: Say Acheson's speech may have encouraged the invasion, never that it caused it. Remember the UN acted because the Soviet Union was boycotting the Security Council, and that the war was never formally declared.

notes.h: Korea: the war, the armistice and the results, 1950 to 1953
notes.b: The war swung up and down the peninsula before settling into a stalemate close to where it began.
points: General Douglas MacArthur led the UN forces. His landing at Inchon on 15 September 1950 cut North Korean supply lines and led to the recapture of Seoul in late September 1950.
UN forces crossed the 38th parallel in October 1950. Chinese forces entered the war in large numbers from late October and November 1950 and drove them back.
Truman dismissed MacArthur on 11 April 1951 after the general publicly argued for attacking China, because Truman wanted the war kept limited. The decision caused a major domestic row.
An armistice was signed at Panmunjom on 27 July 1953 and the frontier stayed close to the 38th parallel. No peace treaty was ever signed, so the two Koreas remained technically at war.
About 36,000 American servicemen died in the war in all. This figure counts non-battle deaths too, so battle deaths were lower.
The results were a stalemate and a limited war. US troops remained in South Korea after the armistice, and the build-up in defence spending urged by NSC-68 went ahead.
notes.tip: When asked about the Korean War's results, give the stalemate and the limit on the war, and use "about 36,000 in all" for American deaths.

notes.h: Cuba, 1901 to 1961: from US dominance to revolution and the Bay of Pigs
notes.b: Cuba lay about ninety miles from Florida, and the United States had long treated it as within its sphere of influence. Castro's revolution ended that, and the quarrel pushed Cuba towards the Soviet Union.
points: Under the Platt Amendment of 1901 the United States had the right to intervene in Cuba. It was repealed in 1934 but left a legacy of US economic dominance, an example of the imperialism Cubans resented.
Fidel Castro's revolution took power on 1 January 1959 after Batista fled, and the new government nationalised (took into state ownership) US-owned sugar, oil and other property in 1960.
Eisenhower retaliated by cutting the Cuban sugar quota in July 1960, imposing a partial trade embargo in October 1960 and breaking off diplomatic relations in January 1961.
Cut off from its main market, Cuba turned to the Soviet Union for trade and oil, which brought Cold War rivalry to the Caribbean.
CIA-trained Cuban exiles landed at the Bay of Pigs on 17 April 1961 and were defeated within three days, a humiliation for Kennedy.
Operation Mongoose, a covert campaign against Castro's government, was authorised in November 1961, which gave Cuba and the Soviet Union reason to fear a further American attack.
notes.tip: Cuba is the commonest Ordinary Level paragraph question, and the sequence from 1 January 1959 to 28 October 1962 earns marks. Don't mix up the Bay of Pigs (April 1961) with the missile crisis (October 1962).

notes.h: The Cuban missile crisis: discovery and the American response, 1962
notes.b: In 1962 the Cold War came closest to nuclear war. It runs from the shipment of the missiles to Kennedy's decision on how to respond.
points: Soviet medium-range missiles were shipped to Cuba from September 1962. Photographs taken by a US U-2 spy plane on 14 October 1962 revealed the launch sites, and Kennedy was shown them on 16 October.
Khrushchev's motives were to defend Cuba from another invasion, to answer US Jupiter missiles in Turkey and Italy, and to offset Soviet weakness in long-range missiles.
Kennedy and his advisers, the Executive Committee (ExComm), rejected an air strike or invasion and chose a naval measure instead.
On 22 October 1962 Kennedy announced on television a naval quarantine of Cuba, meaning US ships would stop and search vessels heading there.
Kennedy said "quarantine" and not "blockade" because a blockade is an act of war in law, so the word kept the move short of war.
notes.tip: On why the crisis began, give Castro, the Bay of Pigs and Khrushchev's motives. On how Kennedy handled it, name ExComm, the options it rejected, and the quarantine, with the reason for the word.

notes.h: The Cuban missile crisis: the climax and the settlement, 1962 to 1963
notes.b: Within a week the crisis reached its most dangerous days and was settled, but only part of the settlement was made public.
points: On 24 October Soviet ships turned back from the quarantine line, so a clash at sea was avoided.
On 27 October ("Black Saturday") a U-2 was shot down over Cuba, killing its pilot, Major Rudolf Anderson, which was the most dangerous day of the crisis.
On 28 October 1962 Khrushchev agreed on Moscow radio to remove the missiles in return for a public US pledge not to invade Cuba.
Kennedy also secretly agreed to withdraw US Jupiter missiles from Turkey. The withdrawal came in 1963, and the deal was kept private for years.
A hotline between Washington and Moscow was installed in 1963, so leaders could talk directly in a future crisis instead of by slow diplomatic messages.
Both sides could claim success. Kennedy got the missiles out and a public victory, while Khrushchev gained a pledge to protect Cuba and the secret removal of the Jupiters.
notes.tip: Marks fall if you give only the public terms, so always give both: the no-invasion pledge and the secret Turkey withdrawal. Keep the dates in order: 22, 24, 27 and 28 October.

notes.h: Vietnam, 1950 to 1960: the French war and Eisenhower's commitment
notes.b: US involvement in Vietnam grew out of the containment of communism in Asia. Johnson's escalation of 1964 to 1968 is a separate case study. There is more on this in the case study on Lyndon Johnson and Vietnam.
points: Vietnam was part of French Indochina, and the Viet Minh under Ho Chi Minh fought the French, who were defeated at Dien Bien Phu in May 1954.
From 1950 Truman gave aid to the French war, and by 1954 the United States was paying about three quarters of its cost, which shows how early the commitment began.
In April 1954 Eisenhower described the domino theory: if Vietnam fell to communism, the rest of Southeast Asia would follow, like a row of falling dominoes.
The Geneva Accords of July 1954 divided Vietnam at the 17th parallel, with elections planned for 1956 that were never held.
The United States backed Ngo Dinh Diem in South Vietnam and joined the Southeast Asia Treaty Organisation (SEATO, an anti-communist alliance for the region) in 1954.
Under Eisenhower the United States trained the South Vietnamese army with a military advisory group, and the first American advisers killed in the conflict died in 1959.
The National Liberation Front, known to the Americans as the Viet Cong, was formed in December 1960 to fight the government in the South.
notes.tip: Vietnam before Johnson is asked as the origins of the war: the domino theory, the 1954 US share of French costs, Diem and the advisers. Keep the Viet Minh (against the French) apart from the Viet Cong (in the South).

notes.h: Vietnam, 1961 to 1963: Kennedy, the Strategic Hamlets and the fall of Diem
notes.b: Kennedy deepened the commitment that Eisenhower had begun, and the weakness of the South Vietnamese government became plain.
points: Kennedy increased US military advisers in South Vietnam to about 16,000 by late 1963, whereas Eisenhower had sent advisers but not combat troops.
Kennedy backed the Strategic Hamlet programme (1962), which moved peasants into fortified villages. It was deeply resented, so it may have helped the enemy more than the government.
In 1963 Diem's persecution of Buddhists provoked protests, including the self-immolation (burning himself to death) of the monk Thich Quang Duc in Saigon in June 1963.
Diem was overthrown and killed in a coup on 2 November 1963, which US officials had tacitly encouraged. After it the South suffered a series of unstable governments.
Diem's fall came three weeks before Kennedy's assassination, so it is easy to mix the two events up.
notes.tip: Name the Eisenhower, Kennedy and Nixon steps separately: Eisenhower sent advisers, Kennedy raised the numbers, and Nixon withdrew troops.

notes.h: Vietnam, 1969 to 1973: Nixon, Vietnamisation, Cambodia and the 1972 offensives
notes.b: Nixon wanted to end US ground fighting without abandoning South Vietnam. His method, Vietnamisation, withdrew American troops but widened the war into neighbouring countries.
points: The Nixon Doctrine, announced at Guam in July 1969, stated that Asian nations should take the main responsibility for their own defence, so the United States would reduce its direct role.
Vietnamisation handed the ground war to the South Vietnamese army while US troops were withdrawn.
US troops numbered about 540,000 at the 1969 peak and had fallen to under 30,000 by late 1972.
Secret bombing of Cambodia, which communist forces used as a base, began in March 1969.
In April 1970 Nixon sent US and South Vietnamese troops into Cambodia to attack communist bases, which sparked protests at home, including Kent State.
In 1971 South Vietnamese forces invaded Laos with US air support and were driven back, which showed the limits of Vietnamisation.
In 1972 Nixon answered North Vietnam's Easter Offensive by mining Haiphong harbour and launching the Linebacker bombing raids, then ordered the Christmas bombing of Hanoi in December 1972.

The Paris Peace Accords were signed on 27 January 1973 and the last US combat troops were out by late March 1973. The fall of Saigon in 1975 came later, and there is more on it in the notes on the decline of Cold War certainties.
notes.tip: Vietnamisation questions ask for its aims, the falling troop figures, Cambodia and the protests, and the 1973 end. Say "at the 1969 peak" for the troop figure.

notes.h: From massive retaliation to flexible response
notes.b: Presidents also had to decide how to use nuclear weapons to support containment, and Eisenhower and Kennedy chose very different strategies.
points: Eisenhower's Secretary of State John Foster Dulles relied on massive retaliation (1954): the threat of nuclear attack to deter communist aggression, which was cheaper than large conventional forces.
Eisenhower is said to have signalled through intermediaries in 1953 that he might use nuclear weapons if the Korean talks failed, though historians dispute how far this forced the armistice.

Kennedy replaced massive retaliation with flexible response, building up conventional and special forces (such as the Green Berets) so the United States could fight limited wars instead of choosing between doing nothing and nuclear war.
After the missile crisis Kennedy and Khrushchev signed the Partial Test Ban Treaty (August 1963), banning nuclear tests in the atmosphere, in space and under water.
notes.tip: Don't confuse massive retaliation (Eisenhower and Dulles) with flexible response (Kennedy). Treat the 1953 nuclear hint in Korea as disputed, not as fact.

notes.h: Key personality: Harry Truman (foreign policy and overall evaluation)
notes.b: Harry Truman became President on Roosevelt's death in April 1945 and faced the start of the Cold War. His domestic record is a separate topic. There is more on this in the notes on US politics and the Presidency.
points: At the Potsdam conference of July and August 1945 Truman met Stalin for the first time, and he authorised the atomic bombings shortly afterwards.
His main achievements were the Truman Doctrine speech to Congress (12 March 1947), the Marshall Plan, NATO and the Berlin airlift, which together contained Soviet power in Europe.
He recognised the new state of Israel on 14 May 1948, within minutes of its declaration of independence, against the advice of parts of his State Department.

He decided in June 1950 to send American forces to defend South Korea without a congressional vote, a decision that set the pattern for later presidential war-making, and he dismissed MacArthur on 11 April 1951 to keep the war limited.

He took the decisions himself: he chose the airlift rather than an armed convoy to Berlin and accepted a limited war in Korea rather than MacArthur's wider war with China. A sign on his desk read "The buck stops here".
Contemporaries were divided: Republicans attacked him over China and spy cases, and by 1952 his popularity had fallen sharply.

Revisionist historians from the 1960s, such as William Appleman Williams, argued that US economic expansion and the atomic bomb helped cause the Cold War. Post-revisionists such as John Lewis Gaddis stressed that Stalin bore great responsibility and that containment worked in Europe.
His reputation has risen since he left office, as later historians judged that his containment policy in Europe worked.
notes.tip: On Truman's foreign policy, give the achievements (Truman Doctrine, Marshall Plan, NATO, airlift, Korea), then the limits (China, the Korean stalemate), and name a historian to add weight.

notes.b: Each president from Truman to Nixon had successes and failures, and judging them means weighing the two against each other.
points: Truman was strongest in Europe, where the Truman Doctrine, Marshall Plan, NATO and the airlift contained Soviet power, but weaker in Asia, where China was lost and Korea ended in stalemate.
Eisenhower relied on massive retaliation, which was cheaper than large conventional forces, but he also began the commitment in Vietnam with aid to France, support for Diem and US advisers.
Kennedy suffered the Bay of Pigs failure and then handled the missile crisis with ExComm and the quarantine, yet he raised the number of advisers in Vietnam to about 16,000.
Nixon cut US troops in Vietnam from about 540,000 at the 1969 peak to under 30,000 by late 1972, but he also widened the war into Cambodia and Laos.

notes.h: Assessment: how successful was US foreign policy to 1972?
notes.b: Judging US policy means setting its successes against its failures, episode by episode, and then deciding how much containment achieved overall.
points: Success in Western Europe: the Marshall Plan, NATO and the Berlin airlift contained Soviet power in Europe and helped to create a prosperous Western alliance.
Failure in Asia: the Korean War ended in a stalemate after about three years, with heavy American losses and no victory.
Korea can also be judged a limited success: South Korea survived, and Truman kept the war from spreading to China or becoming nuclear.

In Cuba the Bay of Pigs was a clear failure, but the missile crisis avoided nuclear war and removed the missiles, although the Jupiters in Turkey were withdrawn as a secret concession alongside the public no-invasion pledge.
Vietnam showed the limits of containment: a commitment that began with aid and advisers had escalated to about 500,000 troops by 1968.
Supporters argue that US commitments in Asia deterred further Soviet and Chinese expansion, while critics say they drew the United States into costly wars in places of little strategic importance.
Contemporaries and later historians differ over whether the Cold War could have been managed by diplomacy earlier, and the debate shapes judgements of Truman, Eisenhower, Kennedy and Nixon.
Korea and Vietnam both came from containment and the domino theory, but the methods differed: a UN force with a declared limit in Korea, and a gradual commitment in Vietnam.
notes.tip: State your verdict in the first sentence and back it with dated evidence from each episode. A strong ranking is Berlin a clear Western success, Korea a limited success or stalemate, Cuba a success with a hidden concession, and Vietnam a failure, all linked through containment.

keyTerms.definition: The policy of active US involvement in world affairs after 1945, in place of the pre-war isolation of the United States.
The domination of one country over others through political, military or economic control, a term applied to US influence in Cuba and to Soviet control of Eastern Europe.
The US policy, set out by George Kennan, of checking Soviet expansion by firm resistance wherever it threatened to spread.
The 1947 commitment to give US aid to free peoples resisting communist pressure, first applied to Greece and Turkey.
The European Recovery Program of 1948 to 1952, which gave about 13 billion dollars in aid to Western Europe to rebuild its economies.
The North Atlantic Treaty Organisation, founded in April 1949 as a military alliance in which an attack on one member is an attack on all.
The Western airlift of supplies into West Berlin from June 1948 to May 1949, which defeated the Soviet blockade of the city.
The October 1962 confrontation over Soviet missiles in Cuba, ended when the Soviet Union removed them in return for a US pledge not to invade Cuba.
The July 1954 agreements that ended the French war in Indochina and divided Vietnam at the 17th parallel.
Eisenhower's 1954 argument that if one Southeast Asian country fell to communism its neighbours would follow, used to justify US involvement in Vietnam.
Nixon's policy from 1969 of withdrawing US troops while training and equipping the South Vietnamese army to fight the war itself.
Kennedy's defence strategy of building conventional and special forces so that the United States could answer communist moves without immediately resorting to nuclear weapons.
Eisenhower and Dulles's 1954 strategy of deterring communist aggression by the threat of overwhelming nuclear response rather than large conventional forces.
The April 1950 National Security Council paper that called for a large build-up of American military strength to contain the Soviet Union.
